traveler: Saint George of Lydda (Georgios, Sant Jordi, San Giorgio, Giyorgis, Jirjis)
title: The Edict, the Dragon and the Tomb at Lydda: George of Cappadocia, from Nicomedia to Lalibela and Lod
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Cappadocia, Nubia, Lydda: the Family the Passio Gives Him

stops.name: Cappadocia, the birth under Aurelian
stops.date_confidence: unrecorded. No source gives a birth year or names the town. The Coptic tradition recovered at Qasr Ibrim places the birth under Aurelian, who reigned 270 to 275; the research pool's geography lens carried 280 instead, with no support. 270 is a placeholder chosen because it at least names an emperor. The pin is the regional centroid the atlas already uses for Cappadocia.
stops.campa: Somewhere in Cappadocia, in a town no text has ever named, a son is born to Gerontius, a Cappadocian Greek in Roman service, and to Polychronia, a Christian woman out of Lydda in Palestine. They call him Georgios, the earth-worker. The only source for any of it is a Coptic manuscript that will lie in the Nubian sand for sixteen hundred years before anyone reads it again. No contemporary of his writes his name down in any language. Every document that names him at all is written by people who never saw him.
suggested_refs: The Qasr Ibrim Coptic manuscript, oldest surviving tradition of George's parentage
sources: Coptic manuscript tradition from Qasr Ibrim, reported via Wikipedia, 'Saint George'

stops.name: Nobatia, the father in the southern garrisons
stops.date_confidence: traditional, and unlocated. Wikipedia's biography section says only that Gerontius served the Roman Empire in Nobatia. No fort, town, unit or year is named in any source consulted. The pin is the modern Aswan area standing in for Lower Nubia, and the date is a placeholder.
stops.campa: The father serves the empire in Nobatia, on the Nile above the first cataract, where Rome's authority thins out into treaty and subsidy and the desert takes over the map. It is the far southern edge of the world George is born into. No source names his post or his unit. The detail gives the family a frontier and gives the frontier three provinces: a Cappadocian in Nubia, a Palestinian wife, a son who will be claimed by Ethiopia and Georgia and England alike. The geography of the cult is already wider than the life.
suggested_refs: The Roman frontier works of Lower Nubia above the first cataract

stops.name: Lydda, the widow comes home
stops.date_confidence: traditional. The Passio has Polychronia return to her native city after Gerontius dies; no source dates the journey and none records it independently. Coordinates unified across all six Lydda stops at the Church of Saint George, Lod, correcting the pool's 31.9515, 34.888.
stops.campa: Gerontius dies and Polychronia takes the boy back to the town she came from, Lydda in Syria Palaestina, a road-junction on the coastal plain, on the route that runs from Jerusalem down to the sea at Jaffa. This is the hinge the hagiographers needed. It puts a Cappadocian in a Palestinian grave, and it hands the later argument over his origins two provinces to fight with instead of one. There is no independent record of the journey. The Passio families do not all agree that it happened.
suggested_refs: Diospolis on the Roman road grid of Syria Palaestina, between Jerusalem and Jaffa

segments.name: Nicomedia: the Court and the Edict

stops.name: Nicomedia, the boy at the court of Diocletian
stops.date_confidence: attested for Constantine, per constantino_el_grande.journey.json, whose pin is inherited here byte-identical. Nothing places George at the same court except tradition.
stops.campa: Diocletian keeps his eastern capital at Nicomedia, palace and mint and guard and tribunal inside one circuit of wall. Into this court the tradition puts a Cappadocian officer named George, risen through the military ranks to the emperor's own bodyguard, a career that gives the later legend its rank and its access: a man positioned to read the persecution edict and tear it down in front of the very palace that issued it, an act the tradition places within days of the posting.
suggested_refs: The imperial palace quarter of Nicomedia, Diocletian's eastern capital

stops.name: Nicomedia, the soldier who sells everything
stops.date_confidence: traditional. Rank and posting differ between recensions of the Passio: some name a tribune, some a comes, some only a man of standing near the guard. No source dates the enlistment or the renunciation.
stops.campa: George is a soldier, and in most tellings an officer of rank in or near the guard. Rank and unit shift from recension to recension, which is what happens to a detail nobody can check. What the families agree on is the renunciation: before he does the thing that will kill him, the soldier gives away what he owns. The Golden Legend, working eight centuries downstream in another language, puts it in one line. One line is all any source ever gives, and the line is repeated because there is nothing behind it to repeat instead.
stops.quote: he left the habit of a knight and sold all that he had, and gave it to the poor
stops.quote_source: The Golden Legend, 'Of Saint George, Martyr', trans. William Caxton (1483)
suggested_refs: The Passio Sancti Georgii recensions on George's military rank
sources: The Golden Legend, trans. Caxton, Fordham Medieval Sourcebook

stops.name: Nicomedia, the church pulled down
stops.date_confidence: attested. Wikipedia's 'Diocletianic Persecution' puts the destruction of the Nicomedian church on 23 February 303, the Terminalia, with the first edict published the following day. The atlas already carries this day, though saint_acacius and constantino_el_grande attach the date to the edict rather than to the demolition.
stops.campa: On the feast of the Terminalia the soldiers come for the church of Nicomedia, which stands in sight of the palace, and take it apart. Scriptures are carried into the street and burned. It is the last day before the persecution has a text to stand on. Nothing in it names George. Everything later attached to him hangs off what goes up on the wall the next morning.
suggested_refs: The cathedral church of Nicomedia, demolished on the Terminalia, 23 February 303

stops.name: Nicomedia, the edict published
stops.date_confidence: attested, and in conflict with three files in this atlas. Wikipedia's 'Diocletianic Persecution' has the church destroyed on 23 February and the first edict published the following day. saint_acacius.journey.json, constantino_el_grande.journey.json and this journey's own research pool all date the edict itself to the twenty-third. The two events are split here rather than merged, and the neighbouring files are left uncorrected.
stops.campa: The first edict goes up in public the morning after the church comes down: churches to be demolished, scriptures surrendered and burned, Christians of rank stripped of office and of the right to answer in a court. It is posted where any literate passer-by can read it, which is the point of posting it. Within weeks the same text is running in Antioch, in Alexandria, in Rome. Fellow Fourteen Holy Helpers Acacius, Cyriacus and Erasmus all die under this same edict. Blaise does not: he dies a decade later, under another emperor.
suggested_refs: The first edict of the Great Persecution, published at Nicomedia, 24 February 303

stops.name: Nicomedia, the hand on the placard
stops.date_confidence: attested as an event, anonymous as to the man. Eusebius, writing within a generation, gives no name, no province and no date beyond the edict's own. The identification with George is later tradition, and the tearing episode is absent from the earliest Greek Acts.
stops.campa: A man of rank, says Eusebius, tears the placard off the wall in front of everyone and is put to death for it. Eusebius was alive, was writing within a generation, and gives no name at all. Three hundred years later the Passio supplies one, and the anonymous man in the Church History becomes George of Cappadocia at the head of his own legend. The earliest Greek Acts do not contain the scene; it arrives late and travels well. This is the entire documentary foundation of the life, and it is a hole with a shape.
stops.quote: a certain man, not obscure but very highly honored with distinguished temporal dignities, moved with zeal toward God, and incited with ardent faith, seized the edict as it was posted openly and publicly, and tore it to pieces as a profane and impious thing
stops.quote_source: Eusebius of Caesarea, Ecclesiastical History VIII.5, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers translation (newadvent.org)
suggested_refs: Eusebius, Historia Ecclesiastica VIII.5, the unnamed man at Nicomedia
sources: Eusebius, Historia Ecclesiastica VIII.5, at newadvent.org

segments.name: Nicomedia: the Torments and the Converted

stops.name: Nicomedia, before the emperor whose name will not hold still
stops.date_confidence: traditional, and contradictory. Most Latin and later Greek recensions name Diocletian; some Eastern recensions name a persecutor called Dadianus; Caxton's Golden Legend runs the trial under a provost named Dacian. Three names across three manuscript families for one scene. Not adjudicated here. The date is a placeholder inside the persecution's first spring.
stops.campa: He is brought up and refuses the sacrifice. Which emperor he refuses is a question the manuscripts will not settle: most Latin and later Greek texts say Diocletian, some Eastern recensions call the persecutor Dadianus, and Caxton's English runs the whole trial under a provost named Dacian with Diocletian and Maximian somewhere behind him. Three names, three families of text, one scene. Offered honours and office if he will sacrifice, George agrees, and walks into the temple in order to bring it down.
stops.quote: Wherefore saidst thou not to me thus at the beginning? I am ready to do as thou sayest.
stops.quote_source: The Golden Legend, 'Of Saint George, Martyr', trans. William Caxton (1483)
suggested_refs: The competing persecutor-names of the Passio families: Diocletian, Dadianus, Dacian
sources: The Golden Legend, trans. Caxton, Fordham Medieval Sourcebook

stops.name: Nicomedia, the wheel, the quicklime, the shoes of iron
stops.date_confidence: traditional, sequence unstable. The Passio recensions disagree on the order and the number of torments; the Catholic Encyclopedia (1913) treats the whole cycle as legendary. The date is a placeholder.
stops.campa: The wheel set with swords turns and does not kill him. He walks in red-hot iron shoes studded with nails and does not die of it. He is buried alive in a pit of quicklime and comes out. The sixth-century Latin Passio counts twenty separate tortures across seven years, with deaths and resurrections between them and forty thousand nine hundred pagans converted along the way. No two recensions agree on the order or the number. The wheel is the one every version keeps, and the one the painters remember.
suggested_refs: The sixth-century Latin Passio Sancti Georgii and its cycle of twenty torments

stops.name: Nicomedia, the myriad martyrs of the eighteenth of March
stops.date_confidence: attested to saint_acacius.journey.json, which itself flags that later calendars confuse this entry with others. The overlap with George's dossier is [R]: no source puts him among these dead or in a cell during them.
stops.campa: On the eighteenth of March the soldiers put a crowd of Nicomedian Christians to the sword, a number the calendars will round up into the Myriad Martyrs and then confuse with three other entries. George's tradition has him in a cell in this city through exactly these weeks, waiting on a governor who keeps offering him a way out he keeps refusing. No source puts him among the dead of this particular day or names him as a witness to it, only as a prisoner under the same roof at the same time.
suggested_refs: The Myriad Martyrs of Nicomedia in the Eastern synaxaria

stops.name: Nicomedia, the enchanter kneels
stops.date_confidence: traditional. The episode is in the Golden Legend and its Latin sources; no date is given anywhere. The placeholder sits late in the imprisonment.
stops.campa: The provost sends for a poison-maker called Athanasius, who mixes the cup twice and twice watches the prisoner drink it and stand up. The enchanter changes sides on the spot and is killed for it the same day. The scene belongs to a stock class of the martyr literature, the magician beaten in public and converted by his own defeat. It is also the only place in the whole dossier where an opponent of George is given a name and a trade, and neither of them makes him any more historical than the man he kneels to.
stops.quote: he kneeled down at the feet of S. George and prayed him that he would make him christian
stops.quote_source: The Golden Legend, 'Of Saint George, Martyr', trans. William Caxton (1483), Fordham text, which reads 'S. George' and is quoted unexpanded
suggested_refs: The magician-versus-martyr contest as a form in the passio literature
sources: The Golden Legend, trans. Caxton, Fordham Medieval Sourcebook

stops.name: Nicomedia, Alexandra baptized in her blood
stops.date_confidence: traditional. Alexandra is the empress in the Latin tradition and the provost's wife in Caxton; her feast exists and is thin, and her historicity rests on the same document as George's and no other.
stops.campa: Watching from the tribunal, the woman the Latin texts call Alexandra declares herself a Christian and asks what becomes of her, unbaptized. She is the empress in some versions and the provost's wife in others, and she dies confessing, before any water reaches her. Her own feast exists in the calendars and is thin. Her historicity is exactly as good as George's, which is to say that it rests on the same document and on no other, and the document is four hundred years late.
stops.quote: Doubt thee nothing, fair daughter, for thou shalt be baptized in thy blood.
stops.quote_source: The Golden Legend, 'Of Saint George, Martyr', trans. William Caxton (1483)
suggested_refs: Alexandra of Nicomedia in the Eastern and Latin calendars
sources: The Golden Legend, trans. Caxton, Fordham Medieval Sourcebook

segments.name: Lydda: the Head, the Grave, the Basilica

stops.name: Lydda, beheaded on the twenty-third of April
stops.date_confidence: traditional, and tagged [R] against two of the three research lenses, which called it attested. No contemporary source names George at all. The 23 April 303 date and the Lydda location are hagiographic tradition first traceable to the Passio literature; Eusebius, the only near-contemporary text in play, names nobody and sets his incident at Nicomedia. Some modern estimates push the martyrdom before 290. Some manuscript families put the execution at Nicomedia and lose the tomb.
stops.campa: They take his head off at Lydda on the twenty-third of April, and the day sticks: Rome keeps it, Constantinople keeps it, Canterbury keeps it, Barcelona sells books on it. In the Golden Legend he asks one thing before the sword falls, and a voice out of the sky grants it. Some manuscript families put the execution back at Nicomedia and lose the grave along with it. The Lydda strand is the one that grew a shrine, and a shrine is the thing that survives a missing document.
stops.quote: that all they that desired any boon might get it of our Lord God in his name
stops.quote_source: The Golden Legend, 'Of Saint George, Martyr', trans. William Caxton (1483)
suggested_refs: The 23 April martyrology entry for George at Diospolis
sources: Donald Attwater, Dictionary of Saints, 3rd ed. (1995), p. 152, via Wikipedia

stops.name: Lydda, the grave and the first veneration
stops.date_confidence: unrecorded, and a correction. The research pool asserted a Constantinian church here, dated 0330 in one lens and 306-337 in another. No fourth-century church at Diospolis is attested anywhere reachable: Wikipedia's 'Church of Saint George, Lod' knows the site's earliest documented building as Byzantine, destroyed in 614. 0310 is a placeholder for local veneration, not a building date.
stops.campa: Local Christians bury him and keep the grave, and the grave is the reason there is a cult at all. No fourth-century church stands over it. The research pool asserted a Constantinian basilica on this ground and it does not exist in any reachable source; what can be said is smaller and firmer. A body is remembered here, locally, before any emperor takes an interest in it. Two centuries on, a pilgrim with a notebook arrives and finds people already coming. The building history starts later than the devotion does.
suggested_refs: The pre-basilical veneration at Diospolis, attested only by what follows it

stops.name: Lydda, Theodosius counts the pilgrims
stops.date_confidence: attested, c. 518-530. Archdeacon Theodosius, De Situ Terrae Sanctae, through Wikipedia's summary; the Latin was not opened this pass, so his exact wording is not established. The pool also claimed the Piacenza Pilgrim recorded the shrine around 570, but his summarized itinerary lists no Diospolis and no George, and that stop was dropped.
stops.campa: The archdeacon Theodosius, writing a working description of the Holy Land for people who mean to travel it, lists Diospolis among the stops and says why: George is there. It is a passing notice in a practical book, and it is the hardest fact in the entire dossier. Two centuries after the traditional death, and long before the dragon or the Garter or the flag, the shrine is already on a route. Whatever George was, the first thing about him that can be verified is a destination.
suggested_refs: Theodosius, De Situ Terrae Sanctae, c. 518-530, on the shrine at Diospolis
sources: Theodosius, De Situ Terrae Sanctae, via Wikipedia, 'Saint George'

stops.name: Lydda, the Sasanids burn the basilica
stops.date_confidence: attested. Wikipedia's 'Church of Saint George, Lod' dates the destruction of the Byzantine basilica to 614, in the Sasanid campaign toward Jerusalem.
stops.campa: The Sasanid armies come up the coast road toward Jerusalem and the basilica at Diospolis goes down with everything else: three aisles, three semicircular apses, a smaller church standing beside it. Archaeology knows the plan and knows the year. What it does not know is what lay under the floor before the fire, or whether anything did. Every later claim to hold the body of George begins after this date, on the far side of a burned building, and none of them can reach across it.
suggested_refs: The three-aisled Byzantine basilica of Diospolis, destroyed 614

stops.name: Constantinople, the palimpsest under the later ink
stops.date_confidence: attested as to Delehaye's identification of a fifth-century text, per Wikipedia; undated and unlocated as to composition. No source consulted says where the palimpsest was written or found. The Constantinople pin is the atlas's Greek-east anchor, used as a declared proxy.
stops.campa: Somewhere in the Greek-speaking east a scribe scrapes a book down and writes over it, and under the later ink lie the oldest surviving lines of George's passion. Hippolyte Delehaye, the Bollandist who spent a career separating what the church could keep from what it had invented, reads them out in the twentieth century and dates them to the fifth. He also judges the deaths and resurrections a later growth. The earliest text of the legend reaches the modern world as the underside of a different book.
suggested_refs: Hippolyte Delehaye's Bollandist analysis of the Greek Acta Sancti Georgii palimpsest
sources: Hippolyte Delehaye, Bollandist scholarship, cited at second hand

stops.name: Rome, the decree that keeps the name and drops the acts
stops.date_confidence: conventionally 494, and softened. The Decretum Gelasianum is generally held pseudonymous, a sixth-century Italian compilation rather than a decree of Gelasius I. The English wording carried here is the Catholic Encyclopedia's rendering; Wikipedia words it differently, and the tertullian.org version renders the clause as passions better known to God than to men. The Latin text was not opened.
stops.campa: A Roman decree on which books may be read sorts the martyrs into two boxes. George goes in the second: honour the name, do not trust the acts. It is the earliest surviving official statement that the story is a story, and it is made by the same authority that keeps the feast. It changes nothing. The cult by now has its own momentum in three languages and four provinces, and the church files the doubt and goes on venerating him for another fifteen hundred years without resolving it.
stops.quote: whose names are justly reverenced among men, but whose actions are only known to God
stops.quote_source: The so-called Gelasian Decree, De Libris Recipiendis, in the Catholic Encyclopedia (1909) rendering, art. 'St. George'
suggested_refs: The Decretum Gelasianum, De Libris Recipiendis, and its list of unvouched passions

stops.name: London, the Syriac fragments Englished
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the c. 600 Syriac version, the British Library fragments and the 1925 English edition, per Wikipedia. The stop is dated to 1925 because that is the only firm date in the sequence; the edition was not opened, so translator, series and shelfmark are gaps.
stops.campa: The fullest early version of the passion is Syriac, made around the year 600, and it survives as fragments that end up on a London shelf. In 1925 someone puts them into English, and the oldest substantially complete George anyone can read turns out to be a translation of a translation, in a language he never spoke, catalogued in a city that has made him its national patron fifteen hundred miles from the tomb. Translator, series and shelfmark are not established here, and the gap is left standing.
suggested_refs: The Syriac Passio of Saint George, British Library fragments, English edition 1925

stops.name: Qasr Ibrim, the oldest parents
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the 1964 recovery and the manuscript's content, per Wikipedia and the Qasr Ibrim excavation reports as summarized there; the reports were not opened, so shelfmark, editor and publication are gaps. The manuscript itself is dated roughly 350 to 500.
stops.campa: Under the rising water of the Aswan dam, salvage archaeologists work a Nubian fortress town and lift out a Coptic manuscript of the fourth or fifth century. In it George has parents: Gerontius the father, Polychronia the mother, a birth under Aurelian, a childhood. It is argued to be the oldest surviving strand of the tradition, and it surfaces in 1964, sixteen centuries after it was copied, in a country that had been keeping his feast on the first of May the whole time without needing it.
suggested_refs: The Qasr Ibrim salvage excavations of the 1960s under the Aswan High Dam campaign
sources: Qasr Ibrim excavation reports, cited at second hand

stops.name: Goreme, the horseman cut into rock
stops.date_confidence: attested as art-historical evidence, tenth and eleventh centuries, per Wikipedia's 'Saint George and the Dragon'. The pin is inherited byte-identical from san_cristobal.journey.json by way of saint_blaise.report.md. No single image is dated to the year.
stops.campa: In the soft rock of the Cappadocian valleys, painters cut churches into cliffs and put a mounted saint on the wall with a spear going down into a serpent. Tenth century, eleventh: these are among the oldest dragon images anywhere, and they are here, in the province the tradition calls his birthplace, not in Libya. Christopher, a fellow Fourteen Holy Helper, is painted in the same rock churches, and his armour and beardless face the guidebooks cannot reliably tell from George's. Soldier saints travel in a crowd and get mistaken for one another.
suggested_refs: The rock-cut cave churches of Goreme and their equestrian saints
sources: Wikipedia, 'Saint George and the Dragon', regional traditions section

stops.name: Tbilisi, the oldest written dragon
stops.date_confidence: attested as an eleventh-century Georgian text, per Wikipedia's 'Saint George and the Dragon'; no year and no place of composition are given, so 1050 is a mid-century placeholder and Tbilisi is a proxy for the kingdom. The 365-churches figure is folkloric, not a count.
stops.campa: The oldest written dragon in the whole dossier is Georgian, eleventh century, two hundred years before the Latin West gets hold of the story. The country that shares his name keeps him hardest: tradition counts three hundred and sixty-five churches of Saint George, one for every day, which is a way of saying everywhere rather than a number anyone has been out and checked. The manuscript's place of composition is not recorded anywhere consulted. Tbilisi here stands in for a kingdom.
suggested_refs: The eleventh-century Georgian text of the dragon legend, oldest known written record

stops.name: Silene in Libya, the girdle and the well
stops.date_confidence: the legend is thirteenth century and the setting is unlocatable. Wikipedia's 'Saint George and the Dragon' says the narrative was first set in Cappadocia in the earliest sources and transferred to Libya only in the Golden Legend. Both settings are carried in this journey and neither is preferred. The pin is Cyrene, an approximation for a medieval 'Libya' that could mean anywhere west of the Nile, not an identification of Silene.
stops.campa: At Silene the dragon has eaten the sheep and started on the children, and the lot has fallen on the king's daughter, who is standing at the water in her wedding clothes when the horseman rides up. He wounds it, has her tie her girdle round its neck, and it follows her back into the town like a dog on a lead. He kills it there, in the square, in front of everybody, on one stated condition. Silene is not a place anyone can find on a map. Libya, in this century, means anywhere west of the Nile.
stops.quote: Fair daughter, doubt ye no thing hereof for I shall help thee in the name of Jesu Christ.
stops.quote_source: The Golden Legend, 'Of Saint George, Martyr', trans. William Caxton (1483)
suggested_refs: The Golden Legend's Silene, unidentified, and the medieval sense of 'Libya'
sources: The Golden Legend, trans. Caxton, Fordham Medieval Sourcebook

stops.name: Genoa, the arm, the cross, the compiler
stops.date_confidence: the Legenda Aurea is conventionally dated c. 1260 and Jacobus de Voragine was archbishop of Genoa; the relic of the arm and the derivation of England's cross from Genoa's ensign are tradition, and the England claim is disputed by historians. Carried unresolved.
stops.campa: Genoa keeps a red cross on white and an arm said to be his, brought back by crusaders, and Genoa is where Jacobus de Voragine, the city's archbishop, assembles the Legenda Aurea and fixes the dragon in the form every later teller inherits. Whether England took its cross from this flag, and paid the republic an annual fee for the use of it, is argued by historians and settled by none of them. The compiler and the ensign sit in the same harbour, the connection left standing where it was found.
suggested_refs: The Genoese ensign of Saint George and the relic of the arm in the cathedral treasury

stops.name: Westminster, Caxton prints him in English
stops.date_confidence: attested. Caxton's English Golden Legend, 1483, printed at Westminster.
stops.campa: William Caxton sets the Golden Legend in English type at Westminster and George becomes readable in the language that will carry him furthest. The chapter opens the way medieval chapters open, by taking the name apart into earth and tilling: the man who works the ground of his own flesh. Every English quotation in this journey comes off Caxton's press. The dragon, the princess, the girdle and the armoured knight enter one nation's imagination through a printer's shop beside the abbey.
stops.quote: George is said of geos, which is as much to say as earth, and orge that is tilling.
stops.quote_source: The Golden Legend, 'Of Saint George, Martyr', trans. William Caxton (1483), opening etymology
suggested_refs: Caxton's 1483 English Golden Legend, printed at Westminster
sources: The Golden Legend, trans. Caxton, Fordham Medieval Sourcebook
catholicsaints.info transcription of the Caxton text

stops.name: Alcoraz, the horseman above Huesca
stops.date_confidence: battle attested, 15 November 1096, per Wikipedia 'Battle of Alcoraz'; the apparition is [R], a legend of the kingdom. Coordinates corrected: the research pool gave 42.1263, -0.4478, which falls southwest of both battlefield and city. The article's own figure is 42 deg 08 min 29 sec N, 0 deg 22 min 57 sec W.
stops.campa: Peter I of Aragon and Pamplona is fighting for Huesca on the fifteenth of November and the tradition says a horseman nobody recruited fights beside him. Aragon takes George for patron afterwards, and the four heads on the Aragonese arms are dated to that same afternoon. The battle is documented and the king is documented. The rider is what a kingdom decided it had seen. A century later Peter II charters a military order under the same patron on the coast at Alfama.
suggested_refs: The battlefield of Alcoraz outside Huesca, 15 November 1096

stops.name: Antioch, three saints in the line
stops.date_confidence: battle attested, 28 June 1098, per Wikipedia 'Battle of Antioch (1098)', which names George, Mercurius and Demetrius in the reported vision. The apparition itself is [R]: the tag is corrected from the pool's chronology lens, which called it attested while its own geography lens said the opposite.
stops.campa: The crusaders come out of the starved city to fight Kerbogha's army, and the chroniclers report three riders in white at the head of the Frankish line: George, Demetrius, Mercurius, the soldier saints of the Greek east, fighting for a Latin army that has just learned their names. The Gesta Francorum is an eyewitness book and its report is attested. What it reports is not. From this day George is a captain and not only a martyr, and the West keeps him in the saddle for eight hundred years.
suggested_refs: The Gesta Francorum on the vision of the three soldier saints at Antioch
sources: Gesta Francorum, c. 1100-1101, cited at second hand

stops.name: Jerusalem, the Temple Mount taken
stops.date_confidence: the fall of Jerusalem, 15 July 1099, is attested; the apparition of George before the city is [R], a chronicler's claim. The pin is the atlas's canonical Jerusalem anchor from richard_lionheart.journey.json, inherited byte-identical, and marks a region rather than a located event.
stops.campa: The city falls in July and the apparitions follow the army: George is said to have shown himself before Jerusalem too. Fifteen miles west, down the road to the sea, lies Lydda, where the head is buried and where the Latins now find, on their first morning as landlords, that their new patron already owns a cathedral in their new country.
suggested_refs: The Temple Mount, taken in the First Crusade's fall of Jerusalem, 1099
sources: Crusader chronicles of the First Crusade, cited at second hand

stops.name: Lydda, the cathedral raised and pulled down
stops.date_confidence: attested. Wikipedia's 'Church of Saint George, Lod' gives the Crusader cathedral rebuilt on the identical Byzantine footprint, roughly 47 by 24 metres, reusing earlier masonry, and demolished by Saladin in 1191, the eastern end with the tomb surviving; the mosque conversion of the ruined western section is Mamluk, fifteenth century. Coordinates corrected from the pool's 31.9506, 34.8892.
stops.campa: On the old Byzantine footprint the crusaders raise a cathedral, forty-seven metres by twenty-four, using the stones already lying on the ground. After Hattin, Saladin has it pulled down, and the eastern end with the tomb is left standing. Two and a half centuries later the Mamluks turn the ruined western half into a mosque, and church and mosque hold the same ground into the present, George on one side of the wall and al-Khadr on the other. Richard the Lionheart is at Jaffa that season, twenty miles off.
suggested_refs: The Church of Saint George and the Great Mosque of Lod on one footprint

stops.name: Al-Khader, the chains near Bethlehem
stops.date_confidence: the Crusader place-name Casale S. Georgii and John Poloner's mention of c. 1421-1422 are attested, per Wikipedia 'Al-Khader'; the imprisonment tradition and the healing chains are local devotion, [R]. Poloner's itinerary was not opened.
stops.campa: South of Bethlehem, in a village the crusaders called Casale S. Georgii, a monastery keeps chains it says were his and lends them to the sick and the possessed. The traveller John Poloner writes the place down around 1421. The imprisonment tradition is local, old and unverifiable; the place-name is documentary. Muslims and Christians both come here, because in this country George and al-Khidr are hard to tell apart and nobody at the shrine has ever needed to separate them.
suggested_refs: The monastery of Saint George at Al-Khader and its chains

stops.name: Fordington, the dedication ascribed to Alfred
stops.date_confidence: traditional, tag corrected from the research pool's [A]. Wikipedia's 'St George's Church, Fordington' gives the fabric late eleventh-century origins, most of the structure twelfth to fifteenth century, three centuries after Alfred's death in 899; Alfred's will (S 1507) concerns the Fordington estate and not a church dedicated to George. The 0899 date marks the tradition's anchor, not a building. Coordinates from the same article.
stops.campa: English devotion says its first church of Saint George stands here, dedicated by the will of Alfred the Great. The building is late eleventh century and most of it is later still, and Alfred's will concerns the Fordington estate and mentions no church of George at all. The dedication is a tradition that got fastened to a king because it wanted one. Bede had already named George among the martyrs a century and a half before Alfred was born, and that mention is the actual first English trace.
suggested_refs: St George's Church, Fordington, Dorset, and the will of Alfred the Great (S 1507)

stops.name: Windsor, the Garter under his banner
stops.date_confidence: traditionally 1348, contested. Wikipedia's 'Order of the Garter' notes that The Complete Peerage puts the first institution at 23 April 1344, with dates from 1344 to 1351 proposed; 1348 is the year of formal proclamation. Carried as 1348 with the contest stated rather than adjudicated. The pool's two lenses differ in the fourth decimal of the longitude, 15 metres apart.
stops.campa: Edward III founds an order of knights and puts it under George: twenty-six stalls, a blue garter, a chapel at Windsor that will eventually hold English kings. The saint stops being one martyr among fourteen and becomes the sign of a monarchy. He is still sharing the patronage of England with Edward the Confessor at this point, and will go on sharing it for two hundred years. What is settled here is the working iconography, in a chapel, around a table of soldiers.
suggested_refs: St George's Chapel, Windsor Castle, and the founding statutes of the Order of the Garter

stops.name: London, the feast raised to a double
stops.date_confidence: attested as an English calendar reform of 1415, per Wikipedia 'Saint George'; the pin is London as a national proxy, not a specific landmark, and the elevation is a process rather than a single dated act at a single place.
stops.campa: The English church raises his day to a festum duplex, the high rank, obligatory across the realm. It is the year of Agincourt, and the army that fights on the twenty-fifth of October is fighting under a saint whose feast had been made a holiday six months earlier. The elevation is calendar administration and it is also a state act. The patron of a chivalric order becomes the patron of the whole country's working year, which is a different and much larger thing.

stops.name: Nuremberg, printed among the saints
stops.date_confidence: attested. Hartmann Schedel's Nuremberg Chronicle, 1493. The pin is the Franconia anchor inherited byte-identical from saint_blaise.journey.json and saint_acacius.journey.json; the Fourteen Holy Helpers are fixed as a company across Regensburg, Bamberg, Wurzburg and Nuremberg by about 1400, per those files.
stops.campa: Hartmann Schedel's chronicle of the world prints George among its saints and the woodcut goes out across Europe in an edition of thousands. Franconia is also where the Fourteen Holy Helpers had been fixed as a company a century earlier, in Regensburg and Bamberg and Wurzburg and this city: Acacius, Barbara, Blaise, Catherine, Christopher, Cyriacus, Denis, Erasmus, Eustace, George, Giles, Margaret, Pantaleon, Vitus. Fourteen and no more. George's portfolio in the company is soldiers, horses, and cattle struck by plague.

stops.name: London, the one banner left standing
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the Edwardian reform, and a correction. The research pool claimed George was formally patron of England by the fourteenth century, supplanting Edward the Confessor. Wikipedia's 'Flag of England' makes him the primary patron only at the Reformation, c. 1552, when the revised prayer book abolished all religious banners except his. The fourteenth century is the cult's rise; the displacement completes here.
stops.campa: Edward VI's reformers strip the banners of the saints out of English use and leave exactly one standing. The red cross on white survives the abolition of the cult that produced it, and George, alone of the fourteen, comes through the Reformation with his flag intact. This, and not the fourteenth century, is when he finishes displacing Edward the Confessor. The process took two hundred years and it ends in a prayer book that has stopped believing the story it is keeping.
suggested_refs: The 1552 revised Book of Common Prayer and the surviving banner of Saint George

stops.name: Kyiv, the church of the eleventh century
stops.date_confidence: traditional. The Russian Orthodox calendar keeps the dedication of a Kyivan church of Saint George on 26 November; the eleventh-century foundation stood near St Sophia and no precise coordinate was verified, so the pin is the city centre. The Bulgarian and Serbian 6 May feast is the 23 April date on the older calendar.
stops.campa: A church of Saint George goes up in Kyiv in the eleventh century, and the Russian calendar keeps its dedication on the twenty-sixth of November, a second feast for a saint who already has April. The Slavic George is a ploughman as much as a soldier: his spring day opens the pasture, and the herds go out under his name from Serbia to the Volga. Bulgaria and Serbia keep him on the sixth of May, which is the same day counted on the older calendar, Gergyovden and Djurdjevdan.
suggested_refs: St George's church at Kyiv and the 26 November dedication feast
sources: Bulgarian and Serbian Orthodox liturgical calendars

stops.name: Lalibela, the church cut downward
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the church and its dedication, thirteenth century, in the Lalibela rock-hewn complex; the tradition that George appeared to King Lalibela demanding it is [R]. 1200 is the conventional turn-of-the-century date for the complex, not a documented year for this church.
stops.campa: At Lalibela the masons do not build. They cut down into the rock and leave a church standing in a pit, shaped as a cross, roofed by its own top surface: Bete Giyorgis, the house of George. Ethiopia keeps him as patron of the nation and of its church. The tradition says the king dug it because George appeared to him and complained that none of the others had been given his name. The building is documented and can be walked into. The complaint is the country's own account of why.
suggested_refs: Bete Giyorgis at Lalibela, monolithic and cruciform, cut downward from the rock
sources: Ethiopian Orthodox tradition and the Lalibela rock-hewn church complex

stops.name: Barcelona, Sant Jordi of the Generalitat
stops.date_confidence: the charter of the Order of Sant Jordi d'Alfama under Peter II of Aragon is dated 1201; the Capella de Sant Jordi in the Palau de la Generalitat and the Diada are later and continuous. The pin is Barcelona. Alfama itself is on the Tarragona coast at l'Ametlla de Mar, and no verified coordinate for the house was obtained this pass, so the two are carried together with the displacement declared.
stops.campa: Sant Jordi is patron of Catalonia and has a chapel inside the seat of its government. The Aragonese line runs back to Peter II, who charters the Order of Sant Jordi d'Alfama in 1201 on the coast south of Tarragona. On the twenty-third of April Barcelona sells books and roses in the street, a civic festival grown out of a church feast and the largest single day in the Catalan book trade. The roses, the tradition says, come from where the dragon's blood soaked into the ground.

stops.name: Moscow, the rider on the shield
stops.date_confidence: no founding date. The research pool gave none and none is documented; the device accretes across centuries of Muscovite and imperial heraldry. 1400 is a declared placeholder set in the period when the rider first appears on Muscovite seals.
stops.campa: Moscow puts him on its shield: a mounted man in armour driving a spear down into a serpent, no dragon named in the blazon, and the same figure sits at the middle of the Russian state arms. No single year founds it. The device accumulates across Muscovite and then imperial heraldry until it is simply there. The city takes as its emblem a Cappadocian who never came within two thousand miles of it, and keeps him through empire, revolution and federation without once revising the drawing.

stops.name: The Phanar, the Patriarchate settles at St George
stops.date_confidence: attested, 1597, corrected from the research pool's 1601. Wikipedia's 'St. George's Cathedral, Istanbul' has Patriarch Matthew II move the Patriarchate to the former convent of St George at the Phanar in 1597, with the Patriarchate's own site dating the seat to about 1600. Coordinates corrected to the article's 41 deg 01 min 45 sec N, 28 deg 57 min 07 sec E.
stops.campa: The Ecumenical Patriarch, moved out of one building after another since the city fell, settles at last in the convent of Saint George at the Phanar, and the church of a soldier martyr becomes the cathedral of Orthodoxy. It has stayed there ever since. The seat of the patriarchate that once crowned emperors is a modest church on a back street above the Golden Horn, under the patronage of a man whose acts Rome had declined to vouch for eleven hundred years before.

stops.name: Lod, the sarcophagus of 1872
stops.date_confidence: attested. The present Greek Orthodox church at Lod was completed in 1872 after Ottoman permission to rebuild; the crypt sarcophagus is venerated as the tomb and the translation is commemorated on 3 November. Continuous physical custody of a body across the site's destructions is tradition, not a documented chain.
stops.campa: The Ottomans permit a rebuilding and the Greek Orthodox raise the present church on the old ground, with a sarcophagus in the crypt venerated as the tomb. The translation of the relics is kept there on the third of November. Whether anything of a third-century body came through the Sasanids, Saladin and the Mamluks is not a chain anyone can document, and the church does not present it as one. The sarcophagus is a place to put a name that has never had an address anywhere else.
suggested_refs: The 1872 Greek Orthodox church at Lod and the crypt sarcophagus

stops.name: Mosul, Nabi Jurjis pulled down
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the destruction, July 2014; the research pool's 27 July is unsupported. Wikipedia's article on the destruction of cultural heritage by the Islamic State gives only the month, alongside Nabi Yunus, and the widely reported day is 25 July. The day is left at 01 as a declared placeholder. Coordinates are approximate for the east-Mosul site and are confirmed in no article consulted.
stops.campa: In Mosul the shrine of the prophet Jirjis, who is George under an Arabic name, stands in a mosque in the eastern city. In July 2014 the Islamic State blows it up, along with the tomb of Jonah, on the argument that shrines are idolatry. The identification of George with al-Khidr and with Jirjis had held in this country for a thousand years, and had been shared at Lod and at Al-Khader by people who prayed in different buildings standing on the same ground.

An Atlantic island parish takes delivery of a bone from a man whose acts the church has declined to certify since the fifth century, and the bells ring anyway.
